scenes.headline: How ssftalk makes a voice
scenes.sub: An ElevenLabs-shaped API over a formant synthesizer
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Coracle! Ssftalk says it is an ElevenLabs engine in pure Rust. Here is how it actually makes a voice.

scenes.text: A voice is a pitch and four formant frequencies shaping a buzzing source, behind request types copied from the ElevenLabs API.
scenes.mark: a pitch and four formant frequencies
scenes.say: There is no neural network here. A voice is a pitch and four resonances shaping a buzz, behind ElevenLabs-shaped requests.

steps.say: A request arrives in the ElevenLabs format. Hand-written letter rules turn the words into phonemes.
The voice is a preset: one pitch, four formants, a tilt and some breath. Even Rachel is six numbers.
A synthesizer shapes a buzz with those resonances. Its source ships encrypted, so I could not read it.

scenes.title: How the hidden code gets built
scenes.say: Four modules are not in readable form.

items.say: The build script reads one encrypted file.
It undoes a simple cipher whose key sits in the script.
It writes out the synthesizer, recognizer, isolation and room code.
Then compiles them in. Ten of the fourteen benchmark stages run that code.

parts.say: Each benchmark stage times a loop of ssftalk calls.
Then divides a number typed into the file. None of the rival tools ever runs.

items.say: The audio language model saving is an amplitude gate. It marks loud samples.
It counts them per frame, but an integer division shifts every frame's window.
On a test second that is ninety percent silence, that gives the eighty-eight percent. Real speech gives far less.

steps.say: Their benchmark table. The baseline column is typed constants, so the headline compares the crate with nothing.

scenes.text: A speedup is only real when both sides run on the same input and machine, with quality reported next to time.

scenes.say: Six numbers. An encrypted synthesizer. Baselines typed in, not run.
